vignette:
She is seventy-four now, a pharmacist who still keeps medicines lined up in her mind with the same precision she once used behind the counter, but when she speaks about her life she does not begin with work. She begins with her husband as a young man, charming in public, quick with compliments, the kind of person her family trusted. In the first years of marriage, she tells herself his temper is stress, then pride, then something she can learn to avoid. She learns the weather of him. She watches the set of his jaw when he comes through the door. She lowers her voice, serves dinner on time, keeps the apartment immaculate, and believes that if she is careful enough she can prevent what comes next.

The first time he hits her, it is over something small and absurd, a misplaced receipt. She remembers not the pain at first but the disbelief, the way the room seems to tilt as if she has stepped off a curb she did not see. He cries afterward, says he is ashamed, says it will never happen again. She wants to believe him because the alternative is too large. She is already working long hours in a pharmacy, standing all day in a white coat, advising strangers how to manage their blood pressure, their infections, their insomnia. She dispenses calm in measured doses while hiding a bruise beneath makeup and the sleeve of her blouse.

The abuse becomes part of the structure of her life. It is not every day, which somehow makes it harder to name. There are stretches of normalcy in which he brings her coffee and asks about her work, and then there are nights when he shoves her against a wall, grips her arms hard enough to leave fingerprints, strikes her with an open hand or a fist. He does it in the kitchen, in the bedroom, once in the garage with the radio playing. She becomes exquisitely attentive to sound. Even now, decades later, she can tell from the cadence of footsteps whether a person is tired, angry, or drunk. Back then, she listens for his key in the door and feels her stomach tighten before she has a conscious thought.

She keeps going to work. At the pharmacy, she takes comfort in routines that make sense: count thirty tablets, check the label twice, verify interactions, ask the customer to repeat the instructions. She likes the fluorescent light, the order of shelves, the authority of facts. Yet the abuse follows her there in quieter ways. If a man raises his voice at the counter, even in ordinary frustration, she feels heat rush to her face and her mind goes blank for a second. When a bottle drops and shatters in the back room, her whole body jerks before she can stop it. Coworkers sometimes tease her for being "jumpy," and she laughs with them, then goes to the restroom and locks herself in a stall until her breathing slows.

She tells no one for years. In her community, marriage is something to preserve, and she carries both loyalty and shame with great seriousness. She tells herself she is protecting her children, protecting the family, protecting her husband from legal trouble, protecting her parents from worry. The cost of this protection accumulates quietly. She sleeps lightly, never fully surrendered to rest. If he turns in bed beside her, she wakes instantly, heart pounding, already bracing. Some nights she stays up in the living room under the excuse of balancing bills, listening for movement. On better nights she dreams she is back in the pharmacy after closing, trying to lock every cabinet while someone pounds on the metal gate outside.

As she gets older, the fear does not fade in the neat way she once hoped. Retirement gives her fewer distractions. Without the daily rhythm of patients and prescriptions, memories arrive with less warning. A certain aftershave in the supermarket, a television scene of a couple arguing, the slap of a cabinet door-these can send her back into the old alertness so quickly that for a moment she is no longer a grandmother choosing avocados but a younger woman calculating how to get through the evening safely. She avoids movies with violence. She sits near exits in restaurants. She startles when her husband enters a room unexpectedly, then feels embarrassed and angry at herself for reacting before she has even looked at his face.

When she speaks about him now, she does so carefully. They are still married, and she does not flatten him into a monster. She remembers his tenderness with their children, his illnesses, his aging body, the years in which the hitting became less frequent. But her own body has not accepted those changes as reassurance. During arguments she feels herself disappear internally, as if a curtain drops between her and the present. Later she struggles to recall what was said. She keeps important papers hidden in the same place she chose decades ago. She checks locks repeatedly at night. She is often tired, irritable, and ashamed of how much of her day is organized around not feeling afraid.

What seems to pain her most is not only what happened, but how thoroughly it shaped her inner life. She spent decades helping others use medicine to control what can be controlled. Meanwhile, in her own home, she lived by anticipation, silence, and the management of danger. Even now, sitting in an office and telling her story in a steady voice, she keeps one ear turned toward the hallway.
